vignette:
Kai stood at the stainless-steel counter of the diner's prep station, his knife moving through a pile of onions with mechanical precision. He could tell the story of what happened that night without hesitating-he had told it to the police, to his ex-wife, to the therapist he saw twice before quitting-but the order of events never held together in his mind. One moment he was wiping down the pass after the dinner rush, the sous chef clapping him on the shoulder in congratulations. The next, he was on the floor of the dry storage room, the smell of garlic and sweat thick in his nostrils, and he was pushing, pushing, but his body would not cooperate. He could not remember how he got from the pass to the floor, or whether the overhead light was on or off. The middle was a dark gap that he had never been able to fill. And when he tried to hold the whole thing in his head, something inside him would slam a door shut, and he would find himself staring at the onions again, the blade moving, his mind blank.

Kai was forty-five, a chef for twenty-two years, and he had always known himself through his hands-the way he could season a broth by instinct, the way a perfect sear felt under his spatula. That was what he was, what he had been. But since the rape, two years ago now, something had curdled. He felt dirty all the time, a greasy film on his skin that no shower could rinse away. When he walked into the diner kitchen each morning, the heat and the clatter of pans felt like an accusation. He was certain that the other line cooks could smell it on him, that they knew what had been done to him, that they saw a man who could be taken apart so easily. He had stopped accepting the evening shift because the dimmer lighting and the smaller crew made his chest seize, and he had stopped working saucier because the garlic-heavy broths brought the taste of that night back into his throat. He took the morning biscuit station instead, safest and most anonymous, and he told the owner it was because his back bothered him.

His marriage had not survived the year that followed. His wife had tried to understand, but Kai could not let her touch him without flinching. He had come to believe that something inside him was irreparably spoiled, that any intimacy would only spread the contamination. She left, and he had nodded because it felt like the natural conclusion. His life had been destroyed-he was certain of that now, the way he was certain of the recipe for hollandaise. The destruction was not dramatic; it was the slow erosion of everything that had made him feel like himself. He no longer experimented with dishes. He no longer took pride in plating. He went to work, he chopped, he went home, he watched television until his eyes burned, and then he did it again.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a Thursday morning when he could not bring himself to open the walk-in cooler. The handle was cold, the light inside was flickering, and the confined space smelled of raw protein and bleach. His legs would not move. He stood in the hallway for ten minutes until a dishwasher asked if he was okay, and then he called in sick and drove straight to the intake office. He was not sure what he hoped for-maybe that someone could help him put the order of events back together, or that they could tell him how to feel clean again. More than anything, he wanted to believe that the man he used to be was still in there somewhere, buried under the grime of what had happened, and that it was not too late to scrub him out.
